title: Adaptive Invoker: cross-runtime streaming + tools SDK examples
creator: Samantha Ortiz
description: Implement and document an "adaptive invoker" SDK pattern that unifies streaming token delivery, function/tool calling, and schema-validated structured output across TypeScript, Python, and Go SDKs. The invoker should support resumable sessions, explicit backpressure/cancellation semantics, and a compatibility layer so older clients can interoperate with new framed JSON events.
acceptance_criteria: TypeScript SDK exposes an AsyncGenerator-based streaming API that yields typed events: token, tool_call_request, tool_call_result, structured_output, and checkpoint
Python SDK exposes an async iterator with equivalent event objects and a helper to resume sessions by checkpoint ID
Go SDK exposes a channel-based stream with context cancellation and clear event enums, plus examples for consuming tool calls inline
Backward compatibility shim converts framed JSON event stream to legacy plain-text streaming for opt-in clients
Integration tests cover tool call lifecycle (request -> external tool invocation -> result injection) and structured output validation against model-provided schema
Docs and code examples for all three languages added to SDK repo with a migration guide
tasks: Design streaming event envelope and versioned schema (ev_v1)
Implement TS SDK invoker and add unit/integration tests
Implement Python SDK invoker and add unit/integration tests
Implement Go SDK invoker and add unit/integration tests
Add compatibility shim for legacy streaming clients
Write developer docs, migration guide, and example apps demonstrating tool calling and structured outputs
Run API review and security review (KMS/tooling access patterns)
design_notes: We adopt an event-envelope approach (ev_v1) so each stream message is a small JSON object with type and payload. Types: 'token', 'tool_request', 'tool_result', 'structured', 'checkpoint', 'error'. Benefits: explicit boundaries for resumability, easier schema validation for structured outputs, and deterministic replay for debugging. Trade-offs: slightly higher token overhead vs. raw streaming; we mitigate by compact envelopes and optional binary frames for kv-cache payloads. Compatibility shim will offer two modes: 'framed' (default) and 'legacy-text' for older clients. Tool calling is modeled as a request/response within the same stream: runtime emits a 'tool_request' event (with tool name, call_id, args), client executes and returns 'tool_result' (call_id). Invoker implementations must support timeouts, retryable tool semantics, and idempotency via call_id. Session checkpoints will include minimal state (call_ids outstanding, kv-prefixes) to allow resumption without full model state transfer. Security: tool_request payloads are redacted in logs unless customer enables expanded audit traces.
py_example:
# Python example: adaptive invoker consumer
from redwood_sdk import AdaptiveInvoker, StreamEvent
import asyncio

async def run():
    inv = AdaptiveInvoker(api_key='${RW_KEY}')
    async for ev in inv.invoke_streaming(model='rw-textrun-1', prompt='Analyze and call tools as needed'):
        if ev.type == 'token':
            print(ev.payload['text'], end='', flush=True)
        elif ev.type == 'tool_request':
            call_id = ev.payload['call_id']
            tool_name = ev.payload['tool']
            args = ev.payload.get('args', {})
            # execute tool synchronously or dispatch to worker
            result = await run_tool(tool_name, args)
            await inv.send_tool_result(call_id, result)
        elif ev.type == 'structured':
            # schema validated payload (dict)
            print('
STRUCTURED:', ev.payload)
        elif ev.type == 'checkpoint':
            persist_checkpoint(ev.payload['id'])

async def run_tool(name, args):
    if name == 'summarizer':
        return {'summary': 'computed summary'}
    return {'error': 'unknown tool'}

asyncio.run(run())
testing_plan: Unit tests for serializer/deserializer of event envelopes (ev_v1)
Integration test with a fake tool runner that injects latency and failures to exercise retry and idempotency
End-to-end tests that validate resumability: start -> checkpoint -> resume -> ensure no duplicated tool effects
Backward compatibility test that toggles legacy-text mode and verifies existing clients still receive a sensible text stream
risks: Tool call deadlocks if client never responds — mitigate with server-side timeouts and explicit failure events
Increased stream overhead may impact high-throughput workloads — mitigate via compact envelope and optional raw token mode
Cross-language subtlety: Python's GIL and synchronous tool execution patterns could block the event loop if users write blocking handlers — docs must emphasize async handlers or executor usage
review_feedback: PM: add a migration guide with snippet to opt-in to legacy-text mode
Design: clarify checkpoint contents and privacy implications (no PII in checkpoints)
Security: ensure tool metadata never contains plaintext secrets; add KMS guidance for tool outputs that need encryption
